q: What does FIGO grade 3 placenta accreta spectrum (percreta) mean?
o: Placenta invading through to the serosa or beyond (e.g. bladder)
why: Grade 1 accreta, grade 2 increta, grade 3 percreta (to serosa, bladder or beyond).

q: What is the main risk factor for placenta accreta?
why: Previous LSCS, other uterine surgery, IVF and age over 35 are risk factors.

q: When is delivery usually planned for placenta accreta spectrum?
o: At 34–36 weeks in a specialist centre
why: Planned at 34–36 weeks with an MDT, IR balloons and preparation for hysterectomy.

q: What proportion of uterine blood flow comes via the ovarian arteries?
why: The uterine arteries (from the internal iliacs) and ovarian arteries (from the aorta, about 35%) both supply the uterus.

q: What is the classic presentation of placenta praevia?
o: Painful bleeding with a hard uterus
why: Painless bleeding, classically around 32 weeks; abruption is painful with a hypertonic uterus.

q: What is Sher stage 3 placental abruption?
o: Intrauterine fetal death, with or without coagulopathy
why: Stage 3 means fetal death; coagulopathy is common, so check fibrinogen.

q: Which test guides anti-D dose after abruption in an Rh-negative mother?
In massive obstetric haemorrhage, which fibrinogen level is targeted?
why: Fibrinogen falls early in obstetric haemorrhage; keep it over 2 g/L, guided by TEG or ROTEM.

q: What is the most common cause of puerperal sepsis?
why: Group A strep; send blood cultures and a throat swab and start broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly (follow local guidelines).

q: In a woman with accreta, why is regional often converted to GA?
o: Pain relief is inadequate for skin incision
Prolonged surgery, massive haemorrhage and hysterectomy
Spinal is contraindicated in all accreta
why: Long surgery with massive bleeding often makes conversion to GA necessary; plan large-bore access and an arterial line.
